pr_body:
This is the first step in an on-going effort to simplify the underlying GrainId type in Orleans.

At this time, we have transitioned the master branch into a development branch for the purpose of faster iteration towards the 4.0 milestone, rather than forking 4.0 from master and having a long-lived development branch. Therefore, this is not intended to be a finished result. Many subsystems still need porting to realize the goal of the new identity type.
pr_comments: Will this new grain identity work also help solve #6308?
Yes, the intention is to decouple interfaces & implementations from identity. This PR is just the first step in that

issue_context.title: Grain state lost when using multiple/generic grain interfaces
issue_context.body:
If a grain is deactivated, then its state can be lost if it's activated through a different interface depending on call order and if the GrainReference interface is generic or not.

Repro: https://github.com/pentp/GenericGrainRef/blob/master/Program.cs
Output:

At this point the grain does not have its state anymore because `Grain.GrainReference` is different while `Identity` is the same as before.

This is really confusing and hard to debug because it depends on activation/call order. Grain state storage should not depend on the way it was activated (called) and Grain.GrainReference value should not change for the same grain.
#1123 might be relevant also.
comments: @pentp It looks like https://github.com/dotnet/orleans/issues/1998 is also a relevant issue. The problem is, I suppose, the type is passed along with the identity (and some other data) to create the identifier in the database. When the type is refactored, it won't match with the new code without a transformation step (which is independent but related to passing the full type information to create a database identifier).

Yes, that looks also relevant. But in this case the grains aren't even generic (they each have a concrete type that is also passed to the storage/reminder providers together with the GrainReference), they just implement a generic interface through which they can be activated. In this situation I would expect the internal GrainReference to not have any genericArguments.
Fixed in 4.0. It is unlikely that we can backport the fix. It's related to how grains themselves are identified

review_comments: This feels like it is trying to be clever. However, because ReferenceEquals already handles the `null==null` case, this amounts to a rather unusual way to say `||`.

This method became redundant when you changed the `.Key` property to actually return `_key` instead of whatever you initially had it return in your earlier versions. (I don't remember if it was the Memory, or the string representation, but either way you changed it, and this appears to be relic now.)
You're right. We will do a cleanup pass once the dust has settled. This is supposed to be a fairly rough PR to simply lay the groundwork

GrainId is a fairly decent sized struct, by my count weighing in at 32 bytes on .Net Core, and potentially up to 48 bytes on the .Net Framework. Given that is is also a readonly struct, it seems like it it is the ideal scenario to use the C# 7.2 `in` feature in various method signatures to avoid copying overhead in cases where a method does not get inlined.
This is a bit ugly of a method name, especially since it is a public method on a public type.
We can probably remove it. The naming convention was carried over, but shouldn't have been

This constructor feels a bit unsafe to just publicly expose. It can easily be used to violate the GetHashCode invariants. I know it is wanted for serialization reasons, but this feels like it should be be private, and publically exposed via an `UnsafeCreate` factory method, to flag it as potentially dangerous if not used correctly. 

Now that I think about it, the other constructor is also unsafe, since the creator could mutate the array after creation. Perhaps both should be exposed via such a factory method? This would also apply to `GrainType` and `GrainId`'s constructors for the same reasons.

I'd argue that they are equally as unsafe as `SpanId.UnsafeGetArray`, for basically the same reason.
The idea is that these will be used for serialization. I will make the constructor private and add an UnsafeCreate method instead.

Cool. Yeah I totally get that serialization needs this for best performance. I was mostly worried about this being a potential foot gun since there is nothing in the signature to indicate it is potentially risky to use if you don't understand the implementation.
What is this for? It seems unused, and with the key being available as a public property, anything that needs this could just as easily do it itself.
Wow. this is a surprisingly low level type to make public. I suppose it is needed if `LegacyGrainId` is public.
That's right and ideally we can hide it or remove it later on the series of PRs

You could use `System.Buffers.Text.Utf8Parser.TryParse` for some basic data types like int, to both get down to zero allocations, and avoid unsafe. (It is available in netstandard2.0 via the same package that provides Span itself.) Sadly it cannot help you get rid of using unsafe if you want to avoid double allocations when creating a string, so it does not allow getting rid of all the unsafe blocks.

If only we had the span overloads for Encodings available in netstandard2.0.
